taxonomy.subtopic: PTH-induced osteoblast RANKL and osteoclast activation

questions.stem_html:
A 54-year-old woman has nephrolithiasis, constipation, and diffuse bone discomfort. Calcium is 11.7 mg/dL, phosphate is low, and parathyroid hormone is elevated. Hand radiographs show subperiosteal bone resorption. Bone biopsy demonstrates increased osteoclast activity.

How does excess parathyroid hormone stimulate the osteoclasts?

options.text_html: It binds directly to mature osteoclasts and opens chloride channels
It suppresses osteoprotegerin secretion by renal tubular cells only
It converts calcitonin into an osteoclast-stimulating peptide
It deposits calcium-phosphate crystals that mechanically erode cortical bone
It binds osteoblast-lineage cells and increases RANKL expression, which promotes osteoclast differentiation

questions.explanation_html: PTH acts on osteoblasts and stromal cells to increase RANKL and reduce the relative brake from osteoprotegerin. RANKL binds RANK on osteoclast precursors and promotes their maturation. Although osteoclast activity rises, PTH exerts the key signaling effect indirectly through osteoblast-lineage cells.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: PTH receptors are expressed primarily on osteoblast-lineage cells rather than functioning as a direct osteoclast activator.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: The critical local RANKL-osteoprotegerin balance is regulated in bone, not solely by renal tubular cells.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Calcitonin and PTH are distinct hormones; PTH does not activate bone resorption by modifying calcitonin.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Crystal deposition is not the mechanism of subperiosteal resorption in hyperparathyroidism.

questions.educational_objective: Explain PTH-mediated bone resorption through osteoblast RANKL expression and osteoclast differentiation rather than direct PTH action on osteoclasts.
